items.text: White vs grey pigeon: What the colour difference really means
items.article: White and grey pigeons belong to the same species, but plumage colour may be linked to subtle differences in behaviour, survival and immunity. Spot a white pigeon and a grey pigeon sitting together, and they may look like entirely different birds. But despite the obvious difference in plumage, both belong to the same species, Columba livia, commonly known as the rock pigeon. So, does their colour indicate differences in behaviour, health or survival? According to Dr Vinod Sharma, Head of Veterinary Services and Director at DCC Animal Hospital, Gurugram, the differences are more nuanced than their appearance suggests. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. First, colour does not make a white pigeon a different species from a grey one. “White and grey pigeons are colour variations of the same species, Columba livia. They can interbreed freely and produce fertile offspring, which is evidence of their common species origin,” says Dr Sharma. Pigeons can display considerable variation in plumage, ranging from the familiar grey and darker patterns to predominantly white birds. “White pigeons are often observed to be less territorially competent and more concentrated in city centres,” says Dr Sharma.

items.text: List of prescription drugs that could see you banned from driving
items.article: Driving while unfit due to drugs is against the law in the UK - even if the medication has been prescribed by your doctor Drivers could find themselves banned from the roads if they get behind the wheel while impaired by drugs - even if those drugs are entirely legal and have been prescribed by their GP. While most people are well aware that drink-driving or driving under the influence of illegal substances is a criminal offence, many motorists may be completely unaware that their lawfully prescribed medication could also land them in serious trouble under certain circumstances. Gov.uk advice reads: "Legal drugs are prescription or over-the-counter medicines . If you're taking them and not sure if you should drive, talk to your doctor , pharmacist or healthcare professional." Officers can pull you over and require you to undertake a 'field impairment assessment'. If they believe you are unfit to drive as a result of drug use, you will be arrested and required to provide a blood or urine sample at a police station. It is absolutely crucial to establish whether any medication you are taking affects your ability to drive safely. If convicted of drug-driving, you could face a minimum one-year driving ban and an unlimited fine. In more serious cases, offenders could be handed a six-month custodial sentence and a criminal record. items.article: This deep-blue gemstone has earned the title of the ‘world’s most cursed diamond’, thanks to the long trail of misfortune and death it has left in its trail. | Trending Tales of cursed diamonds have floated through the corridors of history from time immemorial, but few gemstones have acquired a reputation as dark as that of the Hope Diamond. This deep-blue gemstone, weighing over 45 carat, has earned the title of the ‘world’s most cursed diamond’, thanks to the long trail of misfortune and death it has left in its trail. While it is today on display at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in the United States, the Hope Diamond traces its origins back to India. The Hope Diamond’s recorded history begins in 1666, when French traveller and gem merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier purchased it in India. Tavernier sold it to King Louis XIV of France in 1668. It is commonly accepted that the diamond came from the Kollur Mine of the Golconda region. At that time, India was the “only commercial source of diamonds”, the Smithsonian Museum writes on its website. However, the diamond’s true origins are shrouded in mystery. items.article: Saving for major life goals can be daunting. Utilizing an investment calculator clarifies how much to save monthly by incorporating inflation rates for homes Big goals need big money. A home, a child's degree and a calm retirement all cost lakhs. Most people know this, but few know how much to save each month. An investment calculator can answer that question in minutes. It turns a vague wish into a clear number. This blog shows how to use it, step by step. An investment calculator is a free online tool. You enter a few details. It shows what your money may grow to. It can also work backwards. Enter your goal amount, and it shows how much to save each month. The result is an estimate. It is not a promise. Real returns can be higher or lower. Do this for each goal and check if the total fits your income. Prices always increase every year, implying that whatever costs ₹ 10 lakhs now will cost much more in the future. This is the reason you have to consider the future price, and not the current price.

items.article: Ian Mortimer charts the history of England as seen through the windows of his own new home. Published: 09:45, 20 September 2026 | Updated: 09:45, 20 September 2026 In 2013 the historian Ian Mortimer and his young family moved into an ancient house on the edge of Dartmoor. Mearsdon Manor is, to put it politely, a bit of a hotchpotch. The dining room is 17th century, the hall dates from 1590, and the kitchen, with its Tudor fireplace, still shows its medieval traces. A quick rummage in the archives reveals a bill of sale from 1300. Mash-up: In Mortimer's home the dining room is 17th century, the hall dates from 1590, and the kitchen, with its Tudor fireplace, still shows its medieval traces In this gripping book he sets out to tell the history of England through one medium-sized house and the people who lived in it, including a peasant, a shoemaker, a murderous clergyman and, eventually, a historian. Along the way some old historical cliches get busted. William the Conqueror’s invasion in 1066, for instance, turns out to be comparatively mild for Moretonhampstead, the large village in which Mearsdon Manor (otherwise known as 32 Cross Street) stands. The Anglo-Saxon inhabitants were mostly left to their own devices by their new French-speaking overlords, as long as they toed the line. Anyone found guilty of a felony, though, faced the hideous new punishment of blinding and castration.
